title: Complete beginner looking to build an AI trading bot from scratch – where do I start?
author: Michael231108
selftext:
Hey everyone!  
I’m completely new to algorithmic trading and coding trading bots. I’m starting from literally zero, but I’m genuinely interested in learning how to build an automated trading bot, potentially using AI as part of the process.  
My goal isn’t to find a get-rich-quick solution or blindly copy someone else’s bot. I’d actually like to build my own system, understand how it works, backtest strategies, paper trade it, and eventually see if it can become profitable.  
I have access to AI tools, and I’d like to use them to help me write code, troubleshoot, develop strategies, and gradually build a working bot. However, I don’t really know where to begin, what tools to use, or what the right approach is.  
For those of you who have built your own trading bots:  
If you were starting from scratch today, what would you learn and do first?  
Which platform, programming language and tools would you recommend for a complete beginner?  
What would be the best way to backtest and paper trade before risking real money?  
Are there any open-source projects, tutorials or resources you would recommend?  
I’d really appreciate any guidance, advice or even a roadmap from someone who’s been through this process.  
Thanks in advance!

comments.author: eduard_trades
comments.body:
I started from almost the same place, so here's what I'd do again and what I'd skip.



Python. Not because it's the best, but because every tutorial, library and AI answer assumes it. Freqtrade is a good open-source project to read even if you never use it, because it shows how the parts fit: data, strategy, backtest, risk, execution.



Spend your first weeks on the backtest, not the strategy. My most expensive lesson: a bug in how my backtest handled a moved stop made a losing idea look profitable. Before you trust any result, check three things: does it only use candles that had already closed, does it pay fees and slippage, and does a stop inside a candle get hit the way it would in real life.



Then expect most ideas to barely beat random once costs are in. That's normal, not failure. The skill you're actually learning is killing ideas fast and cheap.



AI is great for writing and explaining code. Be careful letting it invent strategies or judge your backtest. It will happily tell you a result looks promising.



Paper trade on an exchange testnet with the exact same code you'd run live, and write down every fill. The difference between what the bot expected and what it got is your real cost.

comments.author: zulfi001
comments.body: did pretty much this path with crypto so heres what id do again. learn basic python and pandas first, thats 80% of it. then download free historical candles (binance gives them for free) and backtest one dead simple rule in pandas, dont need a fancy framework yet. always add fees and some slippage or the results lie to you. keep the last few months of data hidden and only test on it once at the end. if it still works there, paper trade it live for a while, then real money with an amount you wouldnt miss. ai is great for writing the code but double check its backtests, it happily makes ones that peek at future data

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Starting from zero, I’d do it in this order. First pick one simple idea and write its rules down in plain words, before any code. Then have AI help you turn those rules into code and explain every line, so you understand what it does. Test it on past data with fees included, and check it on a stretch of history you didn’t use to build it. After that, paper trade it for a while and keep sizes small if you go live. Which language you use matters less than that order. Cymetica’s Backtest Labs covers the testing step, since it adds fees and holds out the last part of the history.

comments.author: Prior_Bat5628
comments.body:
I'd start with a tiny test whose answer you can calculate by hand. Give your Python script a few artificial daily bars. On the day the signal turns true the close is $102, the next session opens at $104, and your fixed exit is $105. If the rule waits for the signal bar to close, the simulated gross return is $105/$104 − 1, about 0.96%. A backtest showing about 2.94% took the $102 close. Add one no-signal case and one test with costs. Those three checks give you something to verify when AI changes the code.



Then on real history, write down the exact entry and exit, keep the dates fixed, and compare with buying and holding the same instrument. Paper testing can log signal time and assumed fill separately so you can see where the real feed changes the result.



If you're starting with daily US stocks or ETFs, I’m on the eStockes team and this is the free guest form I use to check a simple rule and its fill assumptions: [https://estockes.com/reality-check?preset=sma20&symbol=SPY&utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=organic\_social&utm\_campaign=rc\_own\_rule\_20261120&utm\_content=ai\_trading\_beginner\_manual](https://estockes.com/reality-check?preset=sma20&symbol=SPY&utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=rc_own_rule_20261120&utm_content=ai_trading_beginner_manual) . You can replace SPY with a ticker you already follow and run once. The tool covers the historical check in that workflow. If you try it, ticker, rule, and what you saw versus holding would be enough for useful feedback.
